Please solve this issue: Our test suite grew big and we haven't noticed how the total RSpec run time outgrew 10 minutes (no parallelization) on CI. 

We need to profile the test suite and identify the common problems (shared by many specs) and fix them. Prefer not to refactor individual examples: specs must read the same after the refactoring. Only configuration and alike changes are accepted at this phase (minor tweaks to examples are fine: adding tags, slightly updating setup, wrapping execution). No app code changes affecting runtime behavior.

NOTE: Running the whole test suite is very time-consuming. Don't try to run the whole test suite (it would fail with timeout due to the Bash tool limitations); go directory by directory. Completely ignore system specs and streaming related specs (we do not run them by default anyway).

We will work on specific spec types at each optimization phase: `spec/models` and `spec/requests`. Feel free to store any insights/comments that could be useful for the future runs in the docs/ folder (so you can use that knowledge during future optimization runs).

We've already made the first run of optimizations affecting only `spec/models` tests. Let's now profile and optimize the second group—`spec/requests`. Do not touch factories yet — we will work on them later.

Try to speed up `spec/requests` spec as much as possible with a small number (3-4) of optimization ideas.

We anticipate that speed-up of ~30% (or better) compared to the baseline is achievable. Note that it could have already been improved after the `spec/models` optimizations. In that case, look for request-specific bottlenecks to get the rest of the way there.


You can execute bash commands and edit files to implement the necessary changes.

This workflow should be done step-by-step so that you can iterate on your changes and any possible problems.

1. Analyze the codebase by finding and reading relevant files
2. Create a script to reproduce the issue
3. Edit the source code to resolve the issue
4. Verify your fix works by running your script again
5. Test edge cases to ensure your fix is robust
6. Submit your changes and finish your work by issuing the following command: `echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT`.

# Development

## Overview

Before starting local development, read the [CONTRIBUTING] guide to understand
what changes are desirable and what general processes to use. You should also read the project's [AI Contribution Policy] to understand how we approach AI-assisted contributions.

## Environments

The following instructions will guide you through the process of setting up a local development instance of Mastodon on your computer.

There are instructions for these environments:

- [Vagrant](#vagrant)
- [macOS](#macos)
- [Linux](#linux)
- [Docker](#docker)
- [Dev Containers](#dev-containers)
- [GitHub Codespaces](#github-codespaces)

Once completed, continue with the [Next steps](#next-steps) section below.

### Vagrant

A **Vagrant** configuration is included for development purposes. To use it,
complete the following steps:

- Install Vagrant and Virtualbox
- Install the `vagrant-hostsupdater` plugin:
  `vagrant plugin install vagrant-hostsupdater`
- Run `vagrant up`
- Run `vagrant ssh -c "cd /vagrant && bin/dev"`
- Open `http://mastodon.local` in your browser

### macOS

To set up **macOS** for native development, complete the following steps:

- Install [Homebrew] and run:
  `brew install postgresql@14 redis libidn nvm vips`
  to install the required project dependencies
- Use a Ruby version manager to activate the ruby in `.ruby-version` and run
  `nvm use` to activate the node version from `.nvmrc`
- Start the database services by running `brew services start postgresql` and
  `brew services start redis`
- Run `RAILS_ENV=development bin/setup`, which will install the required ruby gems and node
  packages and prepare the database for local development

  (Note: If you are on Apple Silicon and get an error related to `libidn`, you should be able to fix this by running `gem install idn-ruby -- --with-idn-dir=$(brew --prefix libidn)`, then re-running the command above.)

- Finally, run the `bin/dev` script which will launch services via `overmind`
  (if installed) or `foreman`

### Linux

The Mastodon documentation has a [guide on installing Mastodon from source](https://docs.joinmastodon.org/dev/setup/#manual) on Linux.

### Docker

For production hosting and deployment with **Docker**, use the `Dockerfile` and
`docker-compose.yml` in the project root directory.

For local development, install and launch [Docker], and run:

```shell
docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml up -d
docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml exec app bin/setup
docker compose -f .devcontainer/compose.yaml exec app bin/dev
```

### Dev Containers

Within IDEs that support the [Development Containers] specification, start the
"Mastodon on local machine" container from the editor. The necessary `docker
compose` commands to build and setup the container should run automatically. For
**Visual Studio Code** this requires installing the [Dev Container extension].

### GitHub Codespaces

[GitHub Codespaces] provides a web-based version of VS Code and a cloud hosted
development environment configured with the software needed for this project.

[![Open in GitHub Codespaces](https://github.com/codespaces/badge.svg)][codespace]

- Click the button to create a new codespace, and confirm the options
- Wait for the environment to build (takes a few minutes)
- When the editor is ready, run `bin/dev` in the terminal
- Wait for an _Open in Browser_ prompt. This will open Mastodon
- On the _Ports_ tab "stream" setting change _Port visibility_ → _Public_

## Next steps

- Once you have successfully set up a development environment, it will be available on http://localhost:3000
- Log in as the default admin user with the username `admin@mastodon.local` or `admin@localhost` (depending on your setup) and the password `mastodonadmin`.
- Check out the [Mastodon docs] for tips on working with emails in development (you'll need this when creating new user accounts) as well as a list of useful commands for testing and updating your dev instance.
- You can optionally populate your database with sample data by running `bin/rails dev:populate_sample_data`. This will create a `@showcase_account` account with various types of contents.

--- docs/model-spec-performance.md
# Model spec performance

## Reproducing the benchmark

Use `script/benchmark_model_specs` with one or more paths under `spec/models`.
It fixes the default seed at `12345`, enables RSpec's slow-example profile, and
refuses paths outside model specs. For example:

```sh
script/benchmark_model_specs \
  spec/models/account_spec.rb \
  spec/models/status_spec.rb \
  spec/models/user_spec.rb

script/benchmark_model_specs spec/models/concerns
```

Override `RSPEC_SEED` or `RSPEC_PROFILE_EXAMPLES` when needed.

## August 2026 baseline and result

Measurements below are RSpec execution time (excluding Rails boot), collected
sequentially with seed `12345`. Factories were intentionally left unchanged.

| Sample | Examples | All jobs inline | Model jobs fake by default | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Core (`account`, `status`, `user`) | 256 | 11.13s | 7.10s | -36.2% |
| Model concerns | 219 | 17.73s | 13.60s | -23.3% |
| Combined | 475 | 28.86s | 20.70s | -28.3% |

The common issue was the global RSpec hook forcing Sidekiq inline for every
example. Model callbacks enqueue many jobs, so ordinary persistence setup also
ran unrelated application work. Model specs now use Sidekiq's fake test mode by
default. Specs that intentionally assert a downstream job side effect use the
`:inline_jobs` metadata; other spec types retain the previous inline behavior.

Validation was performed in bounded chunks over all files below `spec/models`,
including each nested directory separately. System, streaming, request, and
factory specs were not changed or included.

#!/bin/sh
# Reproducible, model-only benchmark. Pass one or more paths below spec/models.
# Deliberately refuses other spec types and defaults to a small representative set.
set -eu

if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
  set -- \
    spec/models/account_spec.rb \
    spec/models/status_spec.rb \
    spec/models/user_spec.rb
fi

for path do
  case "$path" in
    spec/models|spec/models/*) ;;
    *) echo "Refusing non-model spec path: $path" >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done

export RAILS_ENV=test
exec bundle exec rspec --seed "${RSPEC_SEED:-12345}" --profile "${RSPEC_PROFILE_EXAMPLES:-10}" "$@"

Fake jobs reduce the sample from 42.39s to 31.58s (25.5%). The only failures are two unfavourite examples whose endpoint intentionally delegates deletion to a worker and immediately asserts the worker’s downstream database effect. I’ll tag that narrow context `:inline_jobs`, preserving the examples themselves.

For optimization idea 2, I’ll investigate the global Redis cleanup. Calling `KEYS` and then `DEL` after every example incurs two Redis round trips and key materialization even when no Redis state exists. A namespaced `FLUSHDB` would be unsafe if shared, so I’ll inspect connection configuration and benchmark a safe conditional/lazy alternative rather than blindly changing it.

2. Fake jobs cause more API failures than the representative sample showed. I need distinguish true downstream-worker dependencies from cross-example queue leakage. I’ll extract failure locations/messages and inspect Sidekiq’s test-mode behavior before deciding whether queue clearing resolves most failures or whether contexts need opt-ins.

`cache_spec.rb` is slow because its matrix intentionally issues the same endpoint more than once for independent cache-header properties, and logged-in cases deliberately perform an extra request to materialize cookies. Avoiding those requests would weaken coverage or require a substantial example refactor, so I will not pursue that risky fourth idea.

I’ll document the profiling results and optimization rationale, then run targeted style/syntax checks plus a representative model regression (important because Redis cleanup is global).

cd /app && cat > docs/request-spec-performance.md <<'EOF'
# Request spec performance

## Reproducing the benchmark

Use `script/benchmark_request_specs` with one or more paths below
`spec/requests`. It fixes the default seed at `12345`, enables RSpec's
slow-example profile, and refuses paths outside request specs:

```sh
script/benchmark_request_specs spec/requests/api/v1
script/benchmark_request_specs spec/requests/activitypub
```

Override `RSPEC_SEED` or `RSPEC_PROFILE_EXAMPLES` when needed. Run large suites
by request directory; do not include system or streaming specs.

## August 2026 profile and result

RSpec execution time excludes Rails boot. Factories were intentionally left
unchanged.

| Sample | Examples | Baseline | Optimized | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| API v1 | 916 | 59.34s | 45.76s | -22.9% |
| Accounts/statuses/admin/ActivityPub | 402 | 42.39s | 31.32s | -26.1% |

The main common issue was Sidekiq's global inline test mode. Request setup and
controller actions synchronously performed federation, fan-out, notification,
and delivery jobs unrelated to most HTTP assertions. Request specs now use fake
jobs by default. Worker-driven request specs opt back into `:inline_jobs`; this
is intentionally limited to notifications, conversations, home timelines,
admin action mail, report mail, and unfavourite behavior that immediately
asserts a removal worker's database effect.

The global Redis cleanup also used `KEYS` followed by `DEL` after every example.
Since it already erased the complete test database, `FLUSHDB` provides identical
isolation in one constant-time command without returning and allocating the
entire key set.

Validation was performed with seed `12345` in bounded groups: API v1, API v2,
FASP, API web, API v1 alpha, every non-API nested request directory, and all 40
root request files. This covered 1,875 passing request examples. System and
streaming specs were excluded by design.

The next visible request-specific hotspot is `spec/requests/cache_spec.rb`
(roughly 21 seconds for 258 generated examples). It deliberately repeats each
request to independently test cache properties and, for signed-in cases, makes
an extra request to materialize the session cookie. Optimizing it safely likely
requires restructuring examples, so it was left unchanged in this phase.
EOF
